description_full: Bright Horizons Family Solutions Inc. provides early education and childcare, comprehensive back-up care, educational advisory, and other workplace solutions services for employers and families in the United States, Puerto Rico, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Australia, and India. It operates in three segments: Full-Service Center-Based Child Care, Back-Up Care, and Educational Advisory services. The Full-Service Center-Based Child Care segment offers traditional center-based early education and childcare, preschool, and elementary education services. The Back-Up Care segment provides center-based back-up childcare, in-home child and senior care, school-age programs, camps, tutoring, pet care, and self-sourced reimbursed care services, as well as sittercity, an online marketplace for families and caregivers through early education and childcare centers, school-age programs and in-home care providers, the back-up care network, and other providers. The Educational Advisory services segment offers tuition assistance and student loan repayment program management, workforce education, and related educational consulting services, as well as college admissions and college financial advisory services. The company was formerly known as Bright Horizons Solutions Corp. and changed its name to Bright Horizons Family Solutions Inc. in July 2012. Bright Horizons Family Solutions Inc. was founded in 1986 and is headquartered in Newton, Massachusetts.

financial_summary: Bright Horizons Family Solution is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $2.6B market cap on $2.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 6% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 24% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $259M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.82× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 7.0×.

Management returns a meaningful 8.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.2% over 3 years, 14.1% over 5 years and 7.2% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 15.7% a year over five years.

own: Insiders own a modest 1.1%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 8.8% a year to shareholders (8.8% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 4.1% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 32,200 employees, each generates about $91K of revenue, 0.2x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 7.6% a year.
That works out to $8K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.8M (20x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
